newsitem.title: USA: Utah lawmakers blast Clinton on redrock monument.
newsitem.headline: Utah lawmakers blast Clinton on redrock monument.

text.p: Utah lawmakers Tuesday accused President Clinton of playing politics when he designated 1.7 million acres in their state as a national monument and said the law he used should be changed to prevent future abuses.

Administration officials, saying Clinton acted to protect the scenic redrock area from efforts in Congress to free more of it for mining and other development, argued against bills that would curb the president's power under the 1906 Antiquities Act.

"The Antiquities Act ought to be amended because it is so easily abused," Utah Gov. Michael Leavitt told a House Resources subcommittee. Leavitt, a Republican, called Clinton's declaration last September to protect the 1.7 million acres as the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument "a partisan political rally that had been planned and executed as an 'under the cover of darkness' surprise."

Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt and White House environmental adviser Kathleen McGinty fended off accusations from Leavitt and Utah's congressmen that the administration fenced out the state's representatives when Clinton decided to designate the southern Utah area as a national monument.
Babbitt said all but three presidents this century have used the Antiquities Law and he would "personally oppose efforts to undo it."
Clinton used the law to make a national monument of an area larger than Rhode Island and Delaware combined, which contains coal reserves estimated to be worth some $1 trillion.

"The president's focus on southern Utah lands reflected widespread concern that proposed coal mining in the area could irreversibly damage federal lands and resources, including potentially some of the most remote, beautiful, historic and ecologically intact areas in the lower forty-eight (states)," McGinty said.

But several Republicans said the announcement, several weeks before the presidential election, appeared to be a move to please environmentalists. "It was very clear to me that this was a political freight train that had run out of control," Utah Sen. Orrin Hatch testified at the hearing.
Hatch pushed a bill that would require congressional approval for a proclamation of more than 5,000 acres.
